title: Comparative evaluation of single and multiple camera-based pose estimation methods for gait spatiotemporal parameter estimation
content:
by Bethany Weber, Brandon Schoenwether, Tyler Booth, Megan McFarland, Jennifer Britton, Moataz Eltoukhy

Single-camera pose estimation may provide a more accessible approach to measure a person’s walking patterns (i.e., gait analysis) than multi-camera markerless motion capture (MMC), but its validity and test-retest reliability remain unclear. This study evaluated spatiotemporal gait parameters from a single iPad camera against an eight-camera MMC reference system across four visits, two weeks apart. Thirty-six healthy adults (18.7 ± 1.7, ranging 18‒27 years) completed usual-gait, bag-carrying, and phone-use walking conditions. Validity analyses included 458 paired trials from Visit 1 and used repeated-measures and mixed-effects methods. Reliability analyses included 33 participants with complete four-visit data and evaluated absolute agreement of single visit-level measurements. Using repeated-measures correlation, the strongest within-participant association between systems was gait speed (rrm = 0.588), followed by stance duration (rrm = 0.528), cycle time (rrm = 0.515), and cadence (rrm = 0.446; all p < 0.001). Step length, calculated as half of stride length, and stride length showed weaker associations (rrm = 0.327 and 0.328; both p < 0.001), whereas swing duration was not significantly associated (p = 0.599). Independent step length and left−right step-length asymmetry were not evaluated. Mean system differences were small, but significant proportional bias was present for all seven gait variables, indicating that system differences changed with measurement magnitude. Walking condition influenced bias for cadence, gait speed, cycle time, step length, and stride length. Test-retest reliability varied by parameter and condition, with absolute-agreement intraclass correlation coefficients ranging from 0.499 to 0.862. Gait speed demonstrated good reliability across all three conditions, step and stride length demonstrated their highest reliability during the phone condition, and swing duration consistently demonstrated the lowest reliability. These findings support the feasibility of single-camera MMC for selected spatiotemporal gait outcomes, particularly gait speed, when accessibility and reduced equipment requirements are priorities. However, the approaches should not be considered interchangeable. Multi-camera MMC may remain better suited when three-dimensional reconstruction or more comprehensive spatial and temporal characterization is required.
